videos.title: Heel-side turns that stick
videos.description: Weight over the front foot, quiet upper body, and a clean edge change. Ideal first drills for new riders on gentle greens.

notes.abstract: A beginner heel-side turn built on front-foot pressure, a quiet upper body, and an early edge change — not a hard carve yet.
points: Start the turn by loading the front foot before the board tips.
Keep shoulders quiet and looking downhill; avoid twisting the upper body first.
Finish with a clean edge change instead of a skidded wash at the end.
notes.conclusion: If the nose chatters or the turn dies, you are late on pressure or looking across the hill.

videos.title: Linking toe and heel edges
videos.description: How to connect turns without the skid spike. Short tip focused on looking downhill and committing to the new edge.

notes.abstract: How to link toe and heel without the mid-turn skid spike by committing the eyes and the new edge together.
points: Look downhill toward the next turn before you release the old edge.
Commit to the new edge in one smooth tip — no pause on a flat base.
Keep speed moderate on greens while the link becomes automatic.
notes.conclusion: A clean link feels continuous; a spike usually means you flattened too long between edges.

videos.title: First day strap-in checklist
videos.description: Stance width, highbacks, and which foot forward. A calm walkthrough before you hit the bunny slope.

notes.abstract: Pre-ride strap-in checklist: stance, highbacks, and which foot forward so day one starts calm.
points: Confirm lead foot and stance width before you leave the shop or car.
Set highbacks so they support without locking your ankles.
Practice strapping in on flat snow so the first slope is not the first attempt.
notes.conclusion: Most first-day chaos is setup, not technique — fix bindings before you chase turns.

videos.title: How to fall without the drama
videos.description: Sit down early, protect wrists, and get up on the right edge. A short safety intro every beginner should watch once.

notes.abstract: Safer beginner falls: sit early, protect wrists, and stand back up on the correct edge.
points: Choose to sit down early instead of fighting a high-speed washout.
Keep hands off the snow when possible; land on padded areas, not palms.
Stand up onto the uphill edge so you do not slide again immediately.
notes.conclusion: Falling well once is better than ten panicked saves that strain wrists and knees.

videos.title: Carving arcs on blue runs
videos.description: Higher edge angles and angulation once linking is solid. Film from the side so you can check if the board is tracking clean.

notes.abstract: Intermediate carving on blues: raise edge angle and angulation once linking already feels solid.
points: Film from the side to check whether the board tracks or skids.
Build angulation from the ankles and knees, not by folding at the waist.
Hold pressure through the middle of the arc before releasing into the next edge.
notes.conclusion: If the tail washes, you are still skidding — shorten the turn and tip earlier.

videos.title: Park warm-up — 50-50s
videos.description: Box pressure, quiet shoulders, and exiting straight. Good progression before noseslides or boardslides.

notes.abstract: Park warm-up on 50-50s: board pressure, quiet shoulders, and a straight exit before harder slides.
points: Approach with matched speed and a centered, soft stance.
Keep shoulders square to the feature; let the board do the slide.
Exit straight and balanced before progressing to noseslides or boardslides.
notes.conclusion: Warm-ups are progression, not a race — clean 50-50s unlock everything after.

videos.title: Buttering on flats
videos.description: Nose and tail presses with soft knees. Use slow motion to see where the board flexes and when the edge catches.

notes.abstract: Nose and tail butters on flats to feel board flex and catch points in slow motion.
points: Start on soft snow or flats with space to recover.
Press through soft knees and watch where the board flexes.
Release before the edge catches; stop if you feel a sudden grab.
notes.conclusion: Butters teach board feel — if you catch often, press less and move slower.

videos.title: First powder floats
videos.description: Back-foot bias, wider turns, and keeping the nose up. Soft-snow intro without tying you to one mountain.

notes.abstract: First powder intro: back-foot bias, wider turns, and keeping the nose up without a specific mountain.
points: Shift a little more weight aft so the nose stays light.
Open the turn radius; powder punishes quick edge snaps.
Keep speed enough to float, not so much that the nose dives.
notes.conclusion: If you submarine, you are too far forward or too slow — float first, style later.

videos.title: Switch riding confidence
videos.description: Start on greens, quiet the front hand, and accept a wider stance. Builds freestyle and powder options later.

notes.abstract: Building switch confidence on easy greens with a quiet front hand and a slightly wider stance.
points: Start on gentle terrain you already ride well regular.
Accept a wider stance and quieter hands while balance recalibrates.
Link short switch turns before chasing speed or steeps.
notes.conclusion: Switch is a skill bank for freestyle and powder — progress by terrain, not ego.

videos.title: Steep couloir line craft
videos.description: Hop turns, committing to the fall line, and reading firm morning snow. Advanced alpine riding with clear margin notes.

notes.abstract: Steep couloir thinking: hop turns, fall-line commitment, and reading firm morning snow with margin.
points: Use hop turns when the fall line is too steep for a long carve.
Commit downhill; hesitation across the fall line builds speed sideways.
Read firm snow early and leave room for mistakes above hazards.
notes.conclusion: Steeps reward decisive short turns and punish late, long skids.

videos.title: Backcountry kit for day tours
videos.description: Beacon, shovel, probe, splitboard notes, and layering. Compact checklist before leaving the resort boundary.

notes.abstract: Day-tour backcountry kit checklist: beacon, shovel, probe, split notes, and layering before you leave the boundary.
points: Carry and know how to use beacon, shovel, and probe as a set.
Check layers and fuel for the full tour, not only the climb.
Treat resort-boundary exits as a plan with partners, not a casual extension.
notes.conclusion: Gear without practice is theater — rehearse rescue basics before the first tour.

videos.title: Cork 540 progression
videos.description: From straight airs to off-axis spins. Spot the landing early and keep rotation compact off the jump lip.

notes.abstract: Cork 540 progression from straight airs: spot early, keep rotation compact off the lip.
points: Own straight airs and axis control before adding off-axis spin.
Spot the landing early and keep the rotation compact.
Progress jump size only after the axis feels repeatable.
notes.conclusion: Corks punish rushed takeoffs — build the pop and the spot first.

videos.title: Tight tree-line speed control
videos.description: Gap reading, short turns, and density after a dump. Advanced tree skiing technique, mountain-agnostic.

notes.abstract: Tight tree-line control after a dump: read gaps, shorten turns, and manage density.
points: Look for gaps and exits before you enter a dense line.
Use short, controlled turns to keep speed honest.
When density rises, slow the cadence instead of forcing a big turn.
notes.conclusion: Trees are about line choice and tempo — speed without an exit is the real hazard.

resorts.name: Niseko
resorts.summary: Deep powder benchmark with tree runs, night skiing, and village energy.
resorts.intro:
Niseko is less a single resort than a cluster of connected areas on Mt. Annupuri. Expect soft snow, birch trees, and long storm cycles.

Good for riders who already link turns and want powder practice. Not ideal as a pure first-week beginner destination if you need huge gentle greens every day.

Budget leans higher in peak season — lodging and food add up quickly near Hirafu.

resorts.name: Hakuba
resorts.summary: Valley of varied mountains — steeps, trees, and more price range than Niseko.
resorts.intro:
Hakuba spreads across several resorts with different characters: some steep and rocky, some friendlier for intermediates.

Trees and powder are excellent after storms. Night options exist but are more limited than Niseko’s big floodlit faces.

Often a better value than the most famous Hokkaido hubs if you plan carefully.

resorts.name: Chamonix
resorts.summary: Big-mountain alpine terrain, serious steeps, and a town that lives for the mountains.
resorts.intro:
Chamonix is an introduction to high-alpine thinking: exposure, variable snow, and routes that punish casual decisions.

Not a cheap week. Lift access, guides, and lodging reflect the reputation.

Come for steep skiing education and mountain culture — not for wide beginner carpets.

resorts.name: Verbier
resorts.summary: Connected 4 Vallées riding with lively nightlife and premium pricing.
resorts.intro:
Verbier suits confident intermediates and advanced riders who want variety in one ticket.

Off-piste and itineraries are a big part of the draw; hire knowledge if you are new to alpine touring terrain.

Expect Swiss prices — firmly in the not-cheap lane — plus a strong après scene.

resorts.name: Whistler Blackcomb
resorts.summary: Huge vertical, strong park scene, and terrain for almost every level.
resorts.intro:
Whistler Blackcomb is a guide-style resort: greens through expert, park progression, and enough acreage to build a week around one skill.

Night skiing is limited compared with some Japanese hills, but the park and grooming are excellent.

Peak weeks are expensive; shoulder season can feel more reasonable.
